title: Standing Up For Human Dignity, Especially at UnitedHealth Group
subtitle: I can't believe I have to say this.
body_html:
Many of us are upset with Big Health companies. Denial of care is rampant, and no company, statistically, does more of this than UnitedHealth Group. I think their business practices need to change, and I'd like them to change for the better. Today’s article is not about those issues.

This article is about everybody's human dignity, including our fellow humans at United.

Lui- M., who doesn't deserve to have his name used, allegedly committed murder on the streets of New York City. My city, and maybe your city, also? That was terrible enough. We will have to trust due process to address his alleged crimes.

The rest of us, however, and this is very particularly aimed at all the people who cheered for his assassination, need to check ourselves. This was and is shameful. Murder is not the way we can resolve problems in a civil society. We need to…

Stand up for each other.

I know that the political winds have shifted, and bullying is more popular than in recent memory. Here's the thing about standing up to bullies: it will never be cool to stop them in the moment. Bullies, especially successful bullies, are the cool kids. They're using their cool kids status to get what they want through coercion, violence, intimidation, and social pressure.

Today, I'm here to tell you that standing up for people is a virtue. Standing up for others is something we should all aspire to. Not all people are nice, and not all people make good decisions. We don't have to agree with others to advocate relentlessly for their dignity and lives.

Political violence— and make no mistake, Luigi was committing political violence— is the antithesis of good. It leads to more of the same, and we can never trust that it's in the hands of responsible individuals. School bullies? We've had a lot of shootings since Columbine; for example, there's a school shooting every day. This is a nightmare. We need less violence, not more.

Nobody should be shot at.

I can’t believe I have to say this.

We recognize that it happens in war. There are even legal barriers around who can shoot anybody else in the middle of a war. I don't care if you don't like what UnitedHealth Group does. I don't like what United does. I wish it could be different, and I’m committed to working with UnitedHealth or any complex organization to achieve better outcomes. This includes a commitment to good-natured criticism when I feel they are making terrible choices.

But, and I say this with 100% moral clarity, all of you can eat a rotten egg if you think it's defensible to cheer for the murder of someone with whom you disagree.

We don't murder murderers. With capital punishment, which I also disagree with, by the way, we have a remarkable amount of due process between the allegation and the execution of the person. Again, I don't think we should do that either. But if we're not gonna murder the absolute worst people on earth after a substantial due process and still allow for appeals?

Then why the heck are we valorizing the murder of people who are just doing their job? If you don't like their job? That's fine. Build a business that competes with their business, and run them out of town. Use legal remedies. Sue them. I honestly give zero hoots how much you think, “Well, they're murderers, too.” Because no, they're not. People at Big Health companies are doing their job and making difficult choices. Do we want them to make better choices? Do we wish to have a productive conversation that can possibly change anything? We have options. Competing with their business, using perfectly legal strategies to tank their company share price, offering people who work there other jobs, at other firms, where they can do something useful. We have the option of not buying their products. We can educate ourselves about the legal framework in which those products are offered. We have endless opportunities to file class action lawsuits. We can use the state attorneys general of any state where we live to file a complaint. We can file complaints! Every complaint you can imagine. We can write whole newsletters poking fun at their companies.

But never, never, never do we get to advocate for the murder of other human people because it pleases our sensibilities and our need for anger and revenge.

That's disgusting. It's beneath us all.

I've previously made the argument that having only deeply terrified people at major healthcare payors is a lousy plan for all of us. This is because those individuals at the top will live isolated lives, disconnected from the rest of the human experience. If only out of fear for their safety. Fear makes it impossible to make good decisions. It renders people less connected and less empathetic to the rest of our human experience. We need empathy, love, and compassion—because that's what we're asking of them. We're asking for compassion and appropriate practices that are in keeping with a compassionate humanity. By spewing venom at these individuals working in a company with tremendously complex systems and financial realities? We are biting off our collective nose to spite our face.

I'm not particularly religious, but I think somebody said something about hating the sin and loving the sinner. Some people do work that is unvarnished, tremendous evil in the world— mobsters, sicarios, and literal murderers. Some of those people find redemption and go on to do good in the world. People are doing complex work at major healthcare payers, including United, who might be the key to understanding how to unravel this mess. We want them to feel welcomed on the side of Justice, we want them to feel loved, we want them to feel understood, we don't want them to feel afraid. We don't want them hiding in a bunker.

Yesterday, I wrote an article and even mentioned a colleague who worked at UnitedHealth. Then I spoke to that colleague, who explained to me how many death threats everyone there is getting all the time.

I understood that we needed to adjust our course, even and especially as critics. Human dignity comes first. Criticism is valid and needs to continue in good faith, in good nature, preferably with a little bit of humor. Financial and business pressures can be applied. Legal pressure needs to be relentlessly applied to ensure more appropriate business practices. We need to ensure compliance with laws that protect the human dignity of health plan members and respect the fiduciary duty of plan sponsors to those plan members.

But never, and I mean never, can we cheer for the murder of our fellow humans. We should not fail to imagine what it's like to live under that kind of threat. It's gonna be true for a lot of people soon. We should stand up for each other. This means nothing if it doesn’t include people with whom we disagree. We protect the freedom of speech of Nazis and Juggalos who love terrible music. We should protect our vulnerable. We should protect our fellow humans. Right now, people who work at Health Plans are under threat. We need to stand up for their right to live unafraid so they can work with us to improve things. If they commit crimes? That is what jail is for, as well as civil litigation. That is for the courts to determine. We stand against public executions. Ironically, I’m probably also going to get death threats for saying even this.

That's it. There's no good excuse. When other people are advocating violence in our world, we should stand up and say something to the contrary.

I stand with my colleagues at UnitedHealth for their dignity, their lives, and their freedom to live without fear.

Share
